This research paper focuses on the numerical solution of a specific type of random equation known as a distributed control system, specifically the regulation problem. We have developed a finite difference method to solve this system, resulting in a random matrix equation representative of the discrete system. By applying the Kronecker-Newton method to solve the matrix equation, we obtain an iterative algorithm for approximating the solution of the discrete system. We have analyzed this algorithm and determined its mean squared error in relation to the time step and step length. Furthermore, we have derived a convergence rate of $O(1/\sqrt h)$ and $O(\sqrt{\Delta t})$ for the error in both the continuous and discrete sensitivity systems. We have also implemented this algorithm numerically and verified its effectiveness through comparative testing with the exact solution. Additionally, we have utilized this algorithm to solve a system with uncertain parameters represented by random functions, and have analytically proven the convergence of the solution in this case. Finally, we have discussed the application of this algorithm to system where the system and solution are characterized by uncertain parameters represented by random functions, and have proposed a hybrid approach to solving such systems. We have also explored the connection between our algorithm and the existing iterative methods such as the Newton-GMRES method. We have conducted an extensive simulation study to evaluate the performance of this algorithm in relation to several factors including the precision of the initial guess, step lengths, time step, system size, and uncertainty in the system and solution. We have conducted these experiments on both random and deterministic systems, and have analyzed the results to provide valuable insights into the performance of this algorithm and suggestions for its further improvement. We have concluded this research paper by outlining the potential extensions and modifications of this algorithm, and the opportunities for applying this algorithm to the complex systems of interest in the fields of mechanics, physics, and engineering. Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of large-scale anisotropy. At the higher end of our energy range, a specific anisotropy signal was initially reported - namely, a right ascension-based dipolar modulation. To further investigate, we divided the most energetic group into three segments, and discovered that this anisotropy becomes increasingly pronounced with rising energy levels above 4 EeV, exhibiting an energy-dependent pattern that adheres to a power law with an index of 0.79 ± 0.19. We also discovered that the orientation of these anisotropy patterns supports their extragalactic origins, across all energy levels examined. Furthermore, an investigation of quadrupolar components revealed that they lacked sufficient statistical significance. We interpret our findings within the context of theoretical models proposing the distribution of extremely energetic cosmic sources and cosmic magnetic field dynamics. The energy-driven evolution of these anisotropy patterns may be attributed to factors such as field dynamics or changing source distributions, and potentially reflect a critical role of supermassive black hole sinks in the evolution of galaxies. The observed patterns hold implications for the distribution of extremely energetic cosmic sources and cosmic magnetic field dynamics within vast cosmic scales. The energy-dependent anisotropy patterns may also be exploited to gain insights into the energy spectra of individual sources and the overall distribution of cosmic sources. This research focuses on addressing inconsistencies in relational tables that contain missing values and functional dependencies. Unlike traditional approaches that require the removal of inconsistent rows or tables, our goal is to maintain consistency while allowing for the presence of missing values. We achieve this by introducing the concept of "degree of inconsistency," which measures the extent to which a row or table breaches a given set of functional dependencies due to the presence of null values. We then establish criteria for determining when it's beneficial to relax specific dependencies in response to incoming data, considering factors like data quality management priorities and the degree of inconsistency. Furthermore, we investigate ways to formulate queries that account for inconsistencies, proposing solutions for evaluating queries semi-precise, precisely, or taking the degree of inconsistency into consideration. Additionally, we explore extensions to our approaches for handling distributed data and missing relationships defined by referential integrity. The study also delves into the computational costs associated with these operations, offering a complex example to illustrate the proposed solutions in action. We conclude by outlining future research possibilities in this domain. Our proposed Neural Descriptor Fields construct object representations that
incorporate both local and global information by integrating point clouds with
category-specific descriptors. This representation allows for efficient
distinction between identically shaped objects and identifies whether two
objects are the same by comparing their internal structures. In contrast to
traditional approaches that rely on global shapes for recognition, this method
demands less precise modeling of objects. We leverage this representation in
various object comparison tasks, including identifying identical objects and
arranging objects in 3D space according to their features. Our results show that
Neural Descriptor Fields outperform representations based on global shapes in these
tasks. Moreover, we demonstrate that point clouds representing simple objects,
such as spheres and cylinders, as well as more complex objects like the LIDAR
scans of a chair and a nightstand, can be effectively compared using this method.

The position of this singularity, relative to the critical point, is precisely captured by a single factor, (1/N), which equals 1.5, 0.5, and 0.25 for N=1, 2, 4 respectively. Although our analysis is relevant to a scalar field theory with complex symmetry breaking, it is also applicable to vector field theories with spontaneous symmetry breaking, polymerizations, or birth processes. Furthermore, we have determined the (1/N) correction to the position of the edge singularity along the critical line, which equals (1/2)(1/N) times the difference between two fixed points, and is difficult to interpret without additional information. In such situations, the (1/N) expansion fails to provide a useful estimate, and a more precise or alternative approach is necessary to determine the correct value of this quantity. This calculation can be carried out using a variety of methods, including perturbation theory, the $ε$ expansion, or the sine-Liouville field theory. Which of these methods is most appropriate will depend on the specific value of the space dimension, although it is likely that the sine-Liouville field theory provides the most accurate result for the basic (1/N) classes. This prediction can be tested using numerical simulations of self-avoiding random walks or O(N) lattice σ models. In statistics and machine learning, it is frequently essential to establish whether a given optimization method for a particular objective function can be trusted to converge to the desired result. To achieve this, it is necessary to establish a bound on the curvature of the objective function based on the mobility of the optimization method. Previously established guidelines regarding the curvature of the objective function have been primarily derived using a variational approach and the convexity of the replica free energy. In this paper, a new method is introduced that involves using a post-AMP (Advanced Message Passing) variational analysis framework, which provides a more precise measure of the curvature of the objective function. Specifically, a bound on the curvature can be obtained from the L1 norm of a particular matrix, which can be estimated through a non-parametric estimation of the posterior distribution of the optimization method. This estimation can be achieved by employing a library of parametric families of distributions. This approach has several significant advantages, including its broad applicability, as it is not limited to specific optimization methods or models, and it provides a time-dependent bound on the curvature that can be used to validate the reliability of particular optimization methods in specific situations. In the context of the glassy random field model, this approach confirms and extends a previous result regarding the boundedness of the curvature of the TAP free energy. Furthermore, this approach has implications for the validity of the post-AMP variational analysis framework, as it provides a precise condition regarding the curvature of the objective function that is necessary for the validity of the framework. This condition is directly related to the algebraic properties of the matrix that characterizes the curvature of the objective function. In the context of the glassy random field model, this approach also provides a precise explanation for the boundedness of the curvature of the TAP free energy, as it shows that the boundedness of the curvature of the TAP free energy is a consequence of the algebraic properties of the matrix that characterizes the curvature of the objective function, rather than the variational analysis framework itself. In the context of the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model, this approach confirms and extends a previous result regarding the stability of the curved minimum of the TAP free energy. Furthermore, this approach provides a precise explanation for the stability of the curved minimum of the TAP free energy, as it shows that the stability of the curved minimum of the TAP free energy is a consequence of the algebraic properties of the matrix that characterizes the curvature of the objective function, rather than the variational analysis framework itself

While using photometry from stars to monitor the atmosphere may seem uncomplicated for optical astrophysics, achieving a precision of 0.01 for measuring the aerosol depth has been challenging. By taking wide-field photometry over a broad altitude range, the aerosol depth can be determined quickly, regardless of the system's absolute calibration, and even provides calibration as a by-product. Our team used extensive data from the FRAM telescope at the Pierre Auger Observatory and a similar telescope at the Cherenkov Telescope Array site to improve the precision of this technique to a precision of possibly 0.01. To accomplish this, we conducted precise laboratory measurements of the system's response to varying light intensities and spectra to counter the limitations of non-linear CCD detectors under observation conditions. By successfully applying this technique on numerous occasions with precisions ranging from 0.5% to 4.5%, we demonstrated its capability to monitor the aerosol depth at multiple sites, including Danjoudjdj near the Mediterranean Sea, the Cherenkov Telescope Array site at the Haifa, and the FRAM telescope at the Malargue in the Andes Mountains. This approach proved particularly valuable for detecting minute changes in aerosol depth, as low precision makes it less suitable for large-scale aerosol depth surveys. Nonetheless, this technique has vast potential uses, such as monitoring the aerosol depth at multiple sites, detecting minute changes in aerosol depth, and combining it with other techniques like radiometer measurements and satellite data to enhance its effectiveness. Moreover, this approach is easily implementable on existing systems and can be achieved with a simple laboratory setup, making it a straightforward and effective method for monitoring the aerosol depth. Lastly, this technique is suitable for a wide range of applications, including but not limited to atmospheric monitoring at observatories, measuring the aerosol depth around telescopes, and assessing the system's calibration systematically.

Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through clustering of projection points derived from those intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining projection clustering and correspondence learning between 2D-3D points. Specifically, a new network architecture is proposed that generates two sets of 2D points from different views, one of which is clustered to predict the object pose. A proposed correspondence learning module is then employed to enhance point clustering and thus pose estimation accuracy. Experimental results indicate that this proposed architecture outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in the DSO-Zarr dataset and DSO-Kinfu dataset. Moreover, this proposed method excels particularly in estimating the rotation component of the object pose. Code is available at: https://github.com/lingyu-95/DeepHMap++.is.

However, in my paper, I show that the propagator of Langevin dynamics can be re-expressed to highlight the connection between harmonic oscillators and the Hessian matrix of a molecular system, thereby gaining insight into the behavior of complex systems and validating the numerical stability of the re-formulated propagator. Additionally, I introduce a novel method for setting the friction parameter in line with the precision of position or orientation measurements, which is critical in simulations that involve the sampling of complex shapes and surfaces. This new approach should significantly enhance the performance and precision of biomolecular simulations in the near future. Specifically, I demonstrate the benefits of this method in simulations of polymer chains and globular proteins, and show that it yields comparable precision to more advanced algorithms such as Langevin dynamics with multiple time steps, while outperforming the conventional method of setting the friction parameter by a significant margin. Moreover, this method should also be applicable to simulations of softer and more brittle biomolecules, and may be extended to simulate multi-body interactions and surface adsorption. Overall, my results confirm that the re-formulated propagator maintains numerical stability and precision in simulations, and demonstrate that the precision of the simulations can be influenced by changing the mass of the beads in the polymer chain. Furthermore, I also demonstrate the precision and performance of this method in simulations of globular proteins, and show that it yields precise configurations with a relatively small number of time steps. Overall, my paper should provide a foundation for the development of more advanced algorithms of biomolecular simulations in the near future. Lastly, I should note that the re-formulated propagator was previously proposed by Bermond et al. in 2011, and my paper is an extension of that work. Additionally, my paper should be relevant to a broader audience than just biomolecular simulation specialists, and may be of interest to graduate students and researchers in the fields of physics and chemistry. Our new method calculates a variation of eigenvector centrality for multi-layered networks that incorporate node importance across different layers. In these networks, defined by separate interconnected graphs without connections between different layers, the value of a node's centrality is determined by the sum of the values of the connected nodes within each specific layer, similar to traditional eigenvector centrality calculations. Unlike standard approaches, our approach takes into account the relationships between different network layers and their respective impact on the centrality values. Unlike current multi-layer eigenvector centrality frameworks that account for inter-layer connections, our approach uses a separate set of equations that can be solved using a hybrid algorithm. This new algorithm first solves a set of augmented Jacobis iterations, replacing the usual power iteration used in traditional eigenvector centrality calculations. Our method facilitates comparison and combination of diverse node importance metrics across different network layers. Our research also introduces a new consensus-based measure called the Layer Centrality Discrepancy (LCD), characterized by three distinct phases of analysis, and demonstrates LCD's utility in identifying layered network components with inconsistent node importance calculations. Our approach and new LCD measure are validated through realistic multi-layered simulations and real-world data sets. Our research highlights novel insights and recognized advantages over current multi-layered networks frameworks. Our open-source implementation, available for download, includes the algorithm and data sets used in our testing. Our method offers a versatile tool with diverse applications in social network analysis, biology, physics, and security systems. This study investigates how spheres interact with water upon impact, specifically the process known as surface seal that occurs as the sphere enters the water's surface. This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. Empirical rules describing when the splash dome closes ("pinch-off time") generally hold for both slow-moving and fast-moving spheres, yet require further refinement, especially in the middle speed range. Our findings reveal that increased intermediate speeds shorten pinch-off times, and that the width of the splash dome also increases in this range. Furthermore, our data challenge the current assumption that the pinch-off time is directly linked to the 450-degree angular velocity, suggesting this relationship may be influenced by other factors, such as water conditions and sphere surface characteristics. By entering the water at intermediate speeds, larger spheres (diameters 25.4mm to 50.8mm) exhibit greater angular velocities than smaller spheres (diameters 9.5mm to 25.4mm), and these larger spheres experience the surface seal regime more extensively. This phenomenon has been successfully integrated into experimental setups to significantly reduce measurement uncertainties to a minimum. In a breakthrough, researchers have achieved this technique in an external control of interband coupling for the first time, by using a microcavity to control the binding energy of an exciton, even when combined with a strong laser. This achievement enables precise studies of quantum mechanics, with a particular focus on the extremely stable dark state of excitons, where all light is blocked. Normally, this dark state is thought to be stable, but by using the new technique, scientists have discovered that it can be disrupted and that the fluctuations can be massive, much larger than any external influence. This finding has a broader impact, with implications for quantum mechanics, semiconductor physics, and even biology, where it may help understand the behavior of complex systems, from the Earth's climate to the human gene. This technique and this discovery of massive fluctuations in a seemingly stable state could also lead to breakthroughs in advanced material development, with potential applications in fields such as photonics, nanotechnology, and quantum computing. Although this achievement was in a semiconductor system, it may also work in other systems, such as molecules and ions, which could further expand its uses. This research was conducted by a team of scientists from the University of Oldenburg in Germany, the Aalto University in Finland, and the University of Warsaw in Poland. Our investigation focuses on a 2D electronic lattice derived from a non-symmorphic wallpaper group, specifically based on a 2D representation of the non-symmorphic wallpaper group Ngd, which has not been explored in previous studies. By employing a tight-binding model, we have mapped this geometric model into a 2D electronic lattice and discovered all possible Dirac points within the first Brillouin zone. In addition, we have observed that the location of these Dirac points can be adjusted through rotation of the lattice structure, potentially allowing for the creation of a Dirac cone in any desired orientation within the momentum space. Furthermore, we have analyzed all possible lattice dislocations and found that they all correspond to a specific type of topological defect known as a Weyl point, thereby providing a potential means of controlling the topological properties of this lattice through mechanical means. A layer-dependent tight-binding model has also been established for this geometric model, offering insights into its quasi-2D electronic properties and revealing that the band structure can be altered from a hyperbolic to a circular form through increase in layer number. Moreover, we have observed that the formation of a gap occurs at a particular chiral angle, which differs from $\pi$ expected in previous studies of the 2D holographic lattice. In addition to these properties, the model also exhibits topological transition among the various lattice structures, thereby providing a versatile means of controlling its electronic properties. A comparison has been made with a 2D holographic lattice based on the same non-symmorphic wallpaper group Ngd, revealing that both lattices exhibit identical properties, thereby ensuring the generality of these findings. The possible realization of this geometric model using transition metal dichalcogenides has also been explored, along with an investigation into the robustness of the proposed model to various lattice dis-orders. The results presented in this study offer a novel means of controlling the topological properties of a 2D electronic system through mechanical means, based on the geometric structure, which can be achieved using transition metal dichalcogenides. In General Relativity using the Newman-Penrose formalism, the use of bivectors plays a key role in identifying the precise nature of a solution. This review focuses on the fundamental aspects and applications of bivectors within the formalism, specifically exploring their connection to the Weyl curvature tensor's nature. We delve into the principles of the Newman-Penrose formalism, the properties of bivectors, and the related electromagnetic tensor equation. Furthermore, we examine the conservation equations derived from the Bianchi identities, and the implications of these identities on a massless vector field. This review also discusses the Coleman-Goldberg theorem and its equivalent formulations, as well as the cases where a massless gravitational wave can propagate in the presence of matter. We conclude by analyzing the Coleman-Goldberg theorem's constraints on the Weyl tensor's coefficients, and the consequences of these constraints on the curvature tensor index. This index, in turn, determines the conservative or radiative nature of the gravitational field. We hope that this review's in-depth analysis will provide a clear understanding of the complex and intricate aspects of the Newman-Penrose formalism, bivectors, and the Coleman-Goldberg theorem. Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the potential for a quicker and more efficient approach using alone CT scans for the accurate segmentation of esophageal tumors. To this end, we present a novel deep learning-based method called the Dilated Dense Focus Unet, which utilizes a unique combination of dense and focus blocks to enhance feature extraction and improve the accuracy of esophageal tumor segmentation on limited CT scans. To validate our approach, we compared it with the established state-of-the-art methods using two separate datasets, resulting in performance metrics of 84.4%, 73.4% for DICE, 86.4%, and 75.4% for IOU, respectively. These findings were also supported by both qualitative and quantitative analyses of the results. Furthermore, our model demonstrated superior performance when compared to a shallow network, while the necessary training data for our network consisted of relatively small CT scans. In summary, we found that it is possible to accurately identify and outline tumors in CT scans of the esophagus without the need for additional information from other imaging techniques, endoscopic findings, or medical histories. Code-mixed languages encompass the diverse ways different languages are combined in texts, varying from mixed syntax to embedded languages within sentences. This categorization is particularly prevalent among social media content, where significant numbers of users combine languages to convey identity, express cultural affiliation, or simplify communication. Code-mixed texts present an significant challenge for traditional NLP techniques due to lacking standards for spelling, grammar, and syntax. Additionally, modeling these texts is complicated because conventional supervised machine learning methods require large datasets, yet code-mixed data is relatively scarce and difficult to assemble. Despite these obstacles, significant opportunities exist for innovative NLP solutions that can handle multilingual contexts. This article explores current research limitations and outlines potential avenues for exciting NLP innovations that can benefit heavily multilingual societies. Although focused on code-mixed languages, the discussion also touches on related issues that may be applicable to other linguistic combinations. Hence the paper title has been changed to Challenges and Opportunities in Code-Mixed NLP for Multilingual Societies.

Quantifying the quality of automatic image descriptions is crucial for advancing the field, and human-annotated description datasets play a significant role in evaluating and training description generation models. While current evaluation metrics primarily rely on matching words and phrases between images and their corresponding descriptions, they fall short in several aspects. This paper discusses the limitations of these metrics and demonstrates specific examples where these approaches lead to suboptimal performance. Specifically, we analyze the performance of several evaluation metrics, including the recently introduced Description Understanding Score, and provide a novel interpretation of how they measure the overlap between image and description attributes. Furthermore, we explore alternative methods rooted in machine learning and human evaluation of descriptions, and highlight the potential of these approaches in evaluating descriptions. By taking a comprehensive view of evaluation methods, this paper aims to stimulate innovative strategies for evaluating descriptions and interpreting the results of benchmark datasets. Ultimately, a deeper understanding of these issues is necessary to establish universally acceptable standards for evaluating descriptions. This paper is an invitation to fellow researchers to collaborate on addressing these challenges and exploring new avenues in description evaluation. We have made the code available at https://github.com/alegovich/describing-images. Between 2004 and 2016, the population dynamics in the U.S. exhibited an unusual pattern where urban areas experienced significant growth, while rural areas showed a marked decline. This period also saw the rise of social media platforms by which misinformation could spread quickly. Utilizing Reddit comments derived from a large dataset, we analyzed the pace of misinformation dissemination in the U.S. This study found that the speed of misinformation transmission accelerated substantially in rural areas during this period and could be attributed to the demographic changes in the U.S. where aging populations are more susceptible to falling prey to false information. Consequently, the phenomenon we're terming the "Big Geographic Shift" had a noteworthy impact on the dissemination of misinformation, potentially serving as a critical explanation for the spread of false information and similarly dangerous content such as extremist ideologies. By understanding this relationship, we may gain valuable insights into the sources of the spreading of false information and develop more targeted strategies for containing it. Although robotic demonstrations are a natural teaching method, learning from solely observed actions does not take full advantage of audio feedback from the instructor. To effectively incorporate auditory cues present during demonstrations, understanding their underlying content and purpose is essential. This study examines audio inputs from humans instructing robots in a simulated environment using the ManipulaLab platform. Specifically, we are investigating three key aspects: (1) identifying the language elements used in demonstrations, (2) determining the relationship between used language and specific robotic actions, and (3) analyzing how instructors phrase actions in relation to object manipulation. We found that the language used is directly related to the actions being performed and that instructors phrase actions in a specific order, generally from top to bottom and left to right. Our findings provide a foundation for interpreting the auditory feedback presented during demonstrations and could be useful for developing strategies to incorporate spoken language into robotic learning systems. We have established that any such system can be reinterpreted through conformal field theory principles. Specifically, a complex field theory is equivalent to a conformal field theory with a symmetric spin triple operator, potentially along with additional operators that commute with each other under the Lie algebra's action. This classification of complex systems using the Euler-Arnold equations provides a novel Lie algebra-based interpretation, and we have explored various examples, including the Allen-Cahn, Cahn-Hilliard, and Harper equations. Additionally, this framework enables us to identify conserved quantities and determine the conformal field theory's symmetry group. Notably, one-dimensional examples can be straightforwardly analyzed using this method, although in higher dimensions the equation's solvability remains unclear. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Cooperative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multi-target cross-domain recommendation in multiple sparse domains. In contrast to conventional CDR methods, MSDCR considers all participating domains as equally data-poor, thereby simultaneously enhancing the recommendation performance across each domain. We devise a Multi-Domain Separation Network (MDSN) and a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module to augment a user's specific aspect preferences in each domain by transferring complementary preferences from other domains, while maintaining domain-specific uniqueness through adversarial training and dynamically determining the degree of complementarity using GAPE. Additionally, we introduce a Multi-Domain Adaptation Network (MDAN) to capture a user's general, domain-agnostic aspect preference. By integrating the domain-specific aspect preference and the domain-agnostic aspect preference, MSDCR attains a thorough understanding of user preferences across each data-poor domain. The empirical evaluations on real-world datasets unequivocally demonstrate the superiority of MSDCR over state-of-the-art single-domain and CDR models. The proposed approach also achieves a notable performance when compared against conventional multi-domain recommendation models. The code for MSDCR is publicly available at: https://github.com/zhoukai1997/MSDCR.

The solution to a conic equation is a concept fundamental to convex optimization, defined as the smallest alpha value permitting the equation's left-hand side to be deemed feasible when scaled by alpha. This concept is a critical component in several optimization methods, including the use of subgrads to identify the largest possible step size and in results on optimization algorithms, such as the convergence rate of a particular version of the proximal gradient method. Until now, no general formula was available to solve for the solution to a conic equation. This work introduces the function \minimize_conic! which, for the first time, provides an analytical solution to a conic equation given its defining matrix and vector, and also offers an alternative to numerical root-finding tools for determining the solution to a conic equation. This solution can be used in a variety of optimization contexts and is particularly useful in combination with the ConvexJl solver. The formula developed in this research is specifically tailored to the Haiku language and is intended as a contribution to the community of researchers interested in convex optimization. The code developed from this research is part of the Hypatia.jl package, a Julia-based solver for convex optimization problems, and is available under the MLT-License. The package Hypatia.jl also includes the function \minimize_conic! as one of its many features, offering a wide range of conic functions and providing an interface for defining and solving conic equations, with support for multi-alpha solutions, unconditional accuracy, and the option to use the ConvexJl solver. The development of Hypatia.jl has been validated through the use of multiple test cases, including an instance of the classic DRUSO problem and a conic equation based on the Cholesky factorization of a symmetric matrix. The code for Hypatia.jl is accessible via GitHub, with documentation available on the Julia Documentation website. The package Hypatia.jl is compatible with Julia versions 3.7, 3.8, and 3.9, with support promised for Julia version 4. The research underlying Hypatia.jl has been funded through an grant from the Swedish Foundation for Strategic Research, with the grant reference number RFP16-0311. The proposed method involves training a single end-to-end model using three distinct outputs, which in turn enables the distinction of reliable data for both segmentation and post-processing purposes. The quality assessment model has been evaluated and validated using MRI data from six critical anatomical areas, resulting in a 98% accuracy rate in identifying both correct and incorrect data. using drive theory and the control and dynamics framework. We introduce a new

This paper examines the structural, electronic, and magnetic characteristics of GdSn3, CmSn3, and the series GdxCm1-xSn3 ($x = 0.25$, $0.5$, and $0.75$) using a full-potential linearized augmented plane wave method within the generalized gradient approximation+U. We studied the fundamental properties of bulk GdSn3, CmSn3, and GdxCm1-xSn3 materials crystallizing in the AuCu3 structure. Our results match previous experimental and theoretical data on the GdSn3 compound and indicate that CmSn3 and GdSn3 both adopt a type-A anti-ferromagnetic configuration and display metallic behavior. Notably, the magnetic moment diminishes with rising Cm content in the GdxCm1-xSn3 series, and these materials share some key characteristics, rendering them promising for spintronic technology applications. Furthermore, we explored the effects of external stress and strain on the electronic and magnetic properties of these compounds. Lastly, we proposed possible synthesis methods for these materials and identified potential phases of the GdxCm1-xSn3 series based on the Goldschmidt rule and phase diagrams of binary alloys. Lastly, we discussed possible synthesis routes and potential phases of the GdxCm1-xSn3 series and analyzed their phase diagrams and the Goldschmidt rule to understand the material's stability in relation to its composition.

Coxeter groups stemming from buildings of type B possess distinctive root systems characterized by hyperplanes dividing space. These root systems can be further divided into A-type and B-type roots. In 1966, Coxeter established a significant result indicating that a change of basis occurs when a reflection operator is expressed in terms of other operators, with the number of basis changes equivalent to the number of A-type roots between the initial and final spaces. This process is referred to as'simplex transformation'. Previously unpublished work by L. H. Clark reveals that a simplex transformation can be perceived as a permutation of the defining coordinates, with the number of such permutations matching the number of B-type roots. Additionally, this number can be determined as the number of elements within the quotient of the group by its maximal abelian subgroup, following a generalization of Weyl's criterion. This generalization dictates that a root is elementary if and only if its corresponding reflection operator commutes with all other operators. Consequently, a root system is regarded as irreducible if it contains at least one non-elementary root. This study demonstrates that the aforementioned Coxeter result holds in the broader context of complex space, with (non-orientable) projective spaces equivalent to the original space following a simplex transformation. Furthermore, this study clarifies the relationship between the group's actions on the space and the root system, with the orientation-preserving subgroups corresponding to the B-type roots and the whole group equivalent to the symmetric group on the set of defining coordinates. This latter aspect is also achievable through an alternative, more intricate path involving the fundamental theorem of the group. This paper's results specialize to the oriented case, which is equivalent to the case defined by the A-type root system. This particular case was previously established by Coxeter. This study's findings were previously obtained by other authors through alternative methods. This paper's approach, however, is distinct as it derives the results from the generalization of Weyl's criterion and the resulting characterization of the root system as irreducible. This study's results can be further generalized to the hyperbolic space of any dimension, which is equivalent to the (n-dimensional) complex projective space of the same number of dimensions. The weak lensing effect by foreground mass should generally increase the apparent brightness of supernovae, counteracting the dimming caused by cosmological expansion, especially in the distant past. This impact should be most pronounced on Type Ia supernovae with higher maximum brightness. By applying this concept to the Pantheon SN Ia dataset, a detection is made for the first time of a correlation between the amount of dimming and the level of luminosity, with a significant positive slope. Using a new estimator for lensing effects that accounts for the scatter in brightness, the analysis finds that the signal for the most luminous supernovae is ~3.5sigma significant. This finding holds even after eliminating the influence of the Pantheon sample's most heavily lensed supernovae, with a much weaker effect (~1.5sigma) left on the remaining data. The analysis also explores the possibility of a relationship between the host galaxies' properties and the level of lensing effect but finds no indication of this. The study concludes that the primary source of the lensing effect is likely caused by the galactic halos within the Milky Way rather than external structures, given that it is consistent with the expected level of self-lensing. Although this prediction can be confirmed with future SN Ia data that have better brightness measurements, the analysis suggests that the estimated level of lensing effect in the Pantheon sample is ~10% of the total cosmological dimming. Furthermore, by incorporating the lensing effect into the SN Ia cosmology analysis, the recovery of the Hubble constant is found to be ~5% lower than the true value, primarily due to the correlation with the level of luminosity. Finally, the analysis highlights the importance of accounting for the spread in brightness when estimating the lensing effect, as it directly affects the precision of the Hubble constant. Last but not least, the analysis finds that the estimated level of lensing effect in the Pantheon sample is consistent with the expected galactic halo density in the Milky Way, given that it is comparable to the density observed in the solar neighborhood. While silicon is beneficial for optical waveguide applications, it possesses a significant disadvantage - it absorbs strongly in the visible spectrum due to metal impurities, specifically in the 400-500 nm range, where it loses precious energy for computational efficiency. A persistent issue with silicon's contamination has hindered theoretical modeling of its behavior in complex photonic systems. We have discovered two primary types of circle configurations that can be transformed through conversion - a pair of non-intersecting circles and a single circle with an enclosed area. We have also found that any circle configuration on a plane can be achieved by applying a series of conversion operations to one of these two basic forms. Furthermore, our analysis has led to an understanding of conversion in a more general context, where it becomes a fundamental operation that completes a given subset of a plane that is defined by the points where circles intersect. We have also established specific rules that must be followed in this general case, allowing any desired subset to be generated through repeated application of conversion to the initial set of points formed by the circles. A key challenge in modern organ transplantation involves managing the abundance of available kidneys for potential recipients. Unlike liver allocations, kidney donations often exceed the number of people in need, making priority rankings and optimal waiting list strategies crucial for maximizing medical progress. In contrast to existing research, which focuses primarily on listing or prioritization methods, our study aims to investigate the ideal waiting list policy for patients awaiting kidney transplants. By developing an optimal stochastic control approach, we establish an ideal policy standard, which serves as a benchmark for evaluating waiting list performance in real-world settings. Although real-world settings introduce complications, such as varying kidney qualities and different allocation priorities, our research demonstrates that an optimal policy would prioritize transplants from higher-quality kidneys more aggressively than those of lower quality, and prefer larger quantity kidneys more consistently. Furthermore, we demonstrate that, in theoretical scenarios with limited data, the best policy often exhibits remarkable robustness, thereby withstanding various parameter variations. Ultimately, our research provides a precise performance metric, which can be used to assess and compare the effectiveness of different listing and prioritization strategies used in real-world kidney transplantation settings. In doing so, we offer a novel approach for evaluating the efficiency of existing methods, as well as a platform for testing and comparing different listing and prioritization strategies in simulated environments. In particular, we examine and compare two widely accepted listing strategies, the Simultaneous Kidney Transplantation approach, and the Single Kidney Transplantation approach, with the aim of identifying performance differences arising from varying kidney quality, recipient compatibility, and allocation priorities. In the process, we introduce a practical performance metric that can be used to evaluate the overall effectiveness of these and other listing and prioritization strategies used in modern kidney transplantation. This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model, revealing its reliance on Markovian assumptions that provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are generated and capture the essence of frequentist synonyms. We also develop generative models and conduct explicit analyses of commonly used loss functions. To further illustrate the limitations of these models, we create synthetic corpora with varying levels of complexity, demonstrating the ability (or inability) of word2vec to effectively learn these structures. We also empirically assess the capabilities of these models using a substantial financial news dataset covering 12 years and spanning 42 million articles, relying on the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists. Our results show that these models are prone to confusing antonyms as frequentist synonyms and mixing terms with opposing polarities. Notably, our research also uncovers the non-stationarity of financial corpora, revealing time-varying patterns in cosine similarity among polarized words or company names. Our analysis highlights the entangled mixture of semantic and co-occurring word distributions that these models are capturing, posing challenges for their disentanglement. Our work also fosters the integration of external knowledge into these models, suggesting the potential to incorporate financial variables, company names, and sector classifications to enhance the quality of embeddings. Our findings are anticipated to contribute broadly to the understanding of NLP embeddings, with potential applications in finance, such as the development of firm-name embeddings for proxy purposes or the analysis of sector-level cosmology. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghassab/word2vec-dynamics.

This article presents the SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM based IDEA systems as alternatives to our previously proposed optimal wideband waveforming strategy in [1].
Fair-throughput and sum-throughput optimisation problems are defined and formulated.
By leveraging an algorithm that utilizes fixed points, we derive the optimal fair-throughput and sum-throughput values for SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM systems.
A hybrid power allocation and scheduling method is then presented for non-ideal conditions.
Our results show that in ideal conditions, SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM IDEA systems provide the same levels of gain, while in practical scenarios, MISO-OFDM offers additional benefits.
In both ideal and practical scenarios, the hybrid power allocation and scheduling method offers additional gains.
Our results also show that in practical scenarios, the ideal conditions' gain is lower than the MISO-OFDM scenario's gain.
Our previous research indicated that in ideal conditions, MISO-OFDM provides a gain of 15.6\% over SISO-OFDM, which is less than the observed 30\% gain.
Our results can be applied to real-world scenarios, which often operate in non-ideal conditions.

In multiagent systems, an equilibrium is a stable state where no agent can benefit by unilaterally changing their strategy, given the behaviors of other agents. However, an issue with traditional machine learning-based models of agents and equilibria is that they do not provide an underlying explanation for why an agent makes a particular choice, which is a significant limitation in complex systems. To address this challenge, we present a novel approach that combines reinforcement learning with a notion of an explainable equilibrium called a best response to a expected behavior, which is more resilient in dynamic systems than other alternatives while retaining explanatory power. In a simple two-agent example, we demonstrate how our approach unlocks explanatory insights that are difficult to obtain with other methods. Furthermore, we apply our model to a real-world problem involving airline passenger behavior, for which it reveals surprising dynamic patterns that are difficult to discover with other models. And finally, we show that our approach is more efficient and provides better solutions than other methods in a range of multiplayer game scenarios. Integrating datasets from various sources, including flux measurements, deep inelastic scattering data, and lattice QCD results for parton distributions, this framework facilitates the determination of parton distribution functions (PDFs) through a method of minimization. By applying constraints derived from equations relating PDFs to measured outcomes, the framework generates sets of PDFs that best match the available data. This theory-based approach underpins the development of PDF tools like xQGranny, PDF Fitting Toolbox, and Lattice QCD providers of PDF proxies. Ultimately, this framework serves as a foundation for present and future PDF fitting projects.

To enhance the effectiveness of experience replay in addressing conceptional challenges during offline policy optimization, we introduce a new variable to estimate the variance of underlying distributions, and propose a new memory replay buffer structure and protocol. This protocol prioritizes the replay of data points with low variance, allowing for a smaller memory buffer and confirming the significance of variance in offline policy optimization. We further develop a new memory replay buffer sampling technique and a policy optimization algorithm incorporating this technique. Our results show that this algorithm yields superior performance compared to existing baselines, and demonstrates the practical value of our proposed method. We also analyze the proposed algorithm's theoretical properties, and validate the proposed technique through a range of experiments. Our code is available at https://github.com/ChengxiangC/VDEPR.

branching scenarios. To evaluate the diversity of generated text, we introduce a

We investigate the connection between a two-dimensional Gaussian free field and multiple Schramm-Loewner evolutions (SLEs) in the context of statistical mechanics models. Specifically, we consider a random planar lattice graph constructed through a loop-by-loop implementation of the Potts model with K colors and temperature T, defined in a simply connected domain D. As K and 1/T increase, the model transitions from a discrete Ising model to a continuous regime, allowing a coupling with multiple SLEs driven by a discrete log-gas on the real line. We establish that the Asymptotic Discrete Complex Hilbert Space (ADCS), a framework introduced by Dub\'edat and Sheffield, encompasses the coupled field near the outer boundary. In the continuous limit, the coupled field converges to a harmonic measure related to multiple SLEs driven by a continuous log-gas, with associated radial trunk lines and branch points. The convergence of the coupled field also implies the convergence of crossing probabilities and lengths, as well as the statistics of the embedded curves in multiple SLEs. The study relies on a loop-regulated renormalization group approach, a version of the Riemann-Hilbert problem, and the Bethe ansatz, with associated combinatorial results such as the PNG SLE bulk drive, the O'Connell-Yor Merton model, and the ASEP SLE beta bulk drive. The research can be viewed as an extension of the works by Smirnov, Chelkak and Korenkiy, and the first author, among others. The paper also includes a discussion of the transition from discrete to continuous models and the associated change in driving measures from discrete log-gases to beta-Hermite free fields. The results can be further generalized to multiple SLEs driven by random log-gases on compact Riemann surfaces. The study involves a number of abstract combinatorial results, with potential value in the study of random planar maps, the study of the approach via loop-regulated renormalization group, with potential applications in the study of the Schramm-Loewner evolution in domains with the presence of obstacles, and the analysis of the transition from the discrete Ising model to the SLE in the context of statistical mechanics models. Understanding how genomic functions affect disease traits through genome-wide association studies remains complex. Our investigation combined genomic functions, genome-wide association studies, and associated regulatory elements to analyze eighteen human traits. This study took a computational approach to determine the impact of genetic variations on traits by identifying the associated genomic regions and predicting their functional effects. We discovered that the majority of genomic regions influenced by variations have unknown functions, suggesting a need for further study. A significant portion of these regions, between twenty and fifty percent, were found to have potential long-range interactions with active genomic regions. We also found that certain regions with established functions, such as gene regions and repetitive elements, account for a small percentage of genome regions influenced by variations. By examining the characteristics of regions with established functions, we were able to identify patterns of tissue-specific activity and associations with specific protein domains. This study provides a comprehensive map of the genomic regions influenced by variations in eighteen human traits and can be used as a foundation for further investigation into the complex mechanisms of disease traits. We highlight specific examples, such as the relationship between repetitive elements and fusion genes, and the connection between protein-coding regions and large-scale rearrangements that could influence gene expression and stability. We also explore how certain traits, such as blood disorders, may be influenced by changes in long-range interactions with genomic regions that are far from variations, such as megabase-scale alterations. This study includes an interactive web application that allows users to explore the genomic regions influenced by variations in eighteen human traits. This application provides an overview of the characteristics of trait-associated regions, including their functional categories, tissue-specific activity, associated regulatory elements, and potential long-range interactions with active genomic regions. We conclude by discussing how studying the impact of genomic functions on disease traits through genome-wide association studies can be further optimized by reducing false positives and improving analytical methods. This can be achieved by incorporating additional data sources, such as epigenomic data from different cell types and tissues, and through the development of more accurate analytical methods, such as better predictive models of the effects of genetic variations on traits. Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade have led some researchers to suggest a significant population of stellar mass black holes in the region. A statistical model of transient neutron star binary systems is presented, incorporating the distribution of recurrence intervals between outbursts. Contrary to expectations, research on a large sample of such systems reveals that the distribution of recurrence intervals is not significantly influenced by the time frame of observations, and instead, a power law model with a specific index effectively describes this distribution. Furthermore, by analyzing the statistics of outbursts within the Milky Way's center, researchers find that the number of sources with extremely long intervals between outbursts is unexpectedly low, a finding that challenges the hypothesis of the majority of the sources within the region being neutron star binaries. In fact, the data suggest that the majority of the sources within the region are actually black hole binaries, with a significant population of the most persistent type known as the "microquasars". The most persistent of these sources, such as GRS 1716.67-33, are also found to exhibit unusual characteristics that contradict current understanding of black hole binaries. The research was conducted using historical data from various telescopes, including the MAXI, Swift, RXTE, and Chandra. The findings have significant implications for the population of the Milky Way's center and the physics of black hole binaries, and were obtained by analyzing a vast amount of data that was previously untapped. The data used in the research are publicly available, and the analysis methods used are straightforward and reproducible. The model of transient neutron star binary systems and the statistics of outbursts within the Milky Way's center provide a unique and unbiased approach to studying this population. The discovery of the low frequency of the most persistent neutron star binaries within the region also sheds new light on the issue of the absence of any outbursts from the source GRO J1655-40 in the recent past, and the possible causes of this phenomenon. The research into the distribution of recurrence intervals between outbursts has significant implications for the monitoring of the Milky Way's center, and the possible triggers of outbursts, and could be applied to other populations of transient sources. Despite their substantial influence, these effects are often overlooked in solid-state physics studies. This article demonstrates the necessity to incorporate dynamics of electron-phonon and spin-phonon interactions into our theories. In these cases, we show that electron-phonon and spin-phonon interactions can lead to the formation of bound electron-phonon states, phonon-assisted optical selection rules, and spin and orbital momentum polarization of photons and phonons. Our findings suggest that careful consideration of these interactions is crucial for a complete understanding of solid-state materials. This is particularly relevant for developing applications that rely on the controlled scattering of photons and phonons, such as quantum memories and thermal engineering. Our research also provides a framework for incorporating the effects of phonon scattering on electrons and spins in various solids, with potential uses in physics and materials science. Our theoretical analysis is supported by numerical results obtained using a combination of mathematical proofs and computational simulations. Understanding the meaning of conversations relies on grasping the semantics at play.  This paper argues that successful parlance analysis, as well as successful natural language inference analysis for conversations, requires a broad range of semantic varieties, including but not limited to, ontological, lexical, and compositional semantics.  We contend that varied semantic phenomena, such as category-based inferences, lexical substitutions, and embedded pronouns, are often mislabeled as being purely lexical or syntactic in nature. We present a series of examples showcasing the diverse semantic varieties essential for accurate inference analysis in conversations, and also present a new dataset, Semantic Variety in Dialogue, that comprises conversations whose underlying inferences require a broad range of semantic varieties for proper interpretation.  We further present challenges and possible approaches to evaluating the semantic complexity of conversations using various varieties.  We hope this research will contribute to a deeper understanding of the semantics of conversations and provide a framework for developing more effective parlance analysis techniques.  We also hope that this research will encourage other researchers to explore the complexities of conversation semantics and explore the possibilities of incorporating natural language inference into parlance analysis techniques.  We made the dataset available at https://github.com/nyu-dl4oldies/SemanticVarietyInDialogue. The occurrence of sustainable hydrogen burning in very low-mass stars might be impacted by rotation due to the addition of centrifugal force and potential break-up caused by rapid spinning. Computer simulations model rotating low-mass stars with the capability for sustained nuclear reactions, considering a range of rotation rates, rather than slow rotation alone. Using these simulations, we determined the boundaries within which stars could maintain nuclear energy through hydrogen burning. These boundaries varied based on angular momentum. However, above a certain threshold (approximately 8.85 x 10^48 erg s) the boundaries broke into two distinct branches, resulting from objects losing mass and experiencing extreme spin. This research was applied to model the development of sub-stellar objects. Two possible scenarios were modeled: one with external forces gradually slowing the star, mainly controlled by spin-down time, and another where the star spins out of control, ultimately shedding mass and shrinking. In the second scenario, we tracked the development of the remaining core. This study also examined the points at which objects begin and stop sustaining hydrogen burning through rotation-induced mass loss. This occurred when the centrifugal force caused by a rotation-induced mass loss cycle became too great for the star to maintain. This happened at particularly high levels of angular momentum (approximately 5.10 x 10^49 erg s). Nonetheless, below a certain mass threshold (approximately 0.15 solar masses), this breaking point occurred before the hydrogen was depleted. The technique of amplitude analysis in hadron decay studies is quite effective, 
However, this analysis faces challenges arising from requirements for interference 
patterns and overall normalization in decay processes, which are often complicated 
by various experimental limitations, such as missing information about initial 
particle conditions, final state detections, and overall detection efficiencies. 
Without proper consideration of these limitations, determined parameters and 
phases could be inaccurately interpreted, potentially leading to errors in 
physical conclusions drawn from data. 
Therefore, this work emphasizes the significance of thoroughly understanding and 
accounting for experimental effects that influence measurements in amplitude analyses. 
We also outline possible strategies for dealing with various experimental challenges 
and limitations that researchers may encounter in various amplitude analysis contexts. 
The paper presented here can serve as a supplement to existing theoretical and 
mathematical amplitude analysis formalism resources, offering a more comprehensive 
overview of the technique that includes discussion of experimental influences on 
data analysis. The intended audience for this work includes researchers conducting
amplitude analysis in hadron decay processes, as well as developers of experimental
analysis tools for these studies. The discussion presented here is primarily based
on examples from meson decay processes, but the discussion also applies to baryon
decay contexts. The paper consists of three main sections, covering introduction to
amplitude analysis, discussion of effects influencing individual amplitudes and their
relative strengths, and discussion of effects influencing phase relationships between
amplitudes. The paper also includes three additional topics that are relevant to
specific research contexts, including analysis of two-body decay processes, decay
processes with three or more final state particles, and partial reconstruction of
decay processes. The research presented here was motivated by the author's own
experiences analyzing data from the BaBar experiment at the SLAC Accelerator Facility. 
The intended purpose of this paper is to provide a starting point for discussion and
potential collaboration with other researchers who have had similar experiences. 
The paper is organized to allow direct access to specific content for researchers
with particular research interests.

the National Science Foundation.

analytical tools used to develop the research presented here.

Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intensive, yet might not always guarantee sufficiently low crossings levels to maintain the visualization's clarity. In contrast, an approach has been developed to remove edge crossings by splitting specific nodes, targeting the minimum number required to yield an edge-free (planar) drawing. The question of determining if an edge-free representation exists after breaking at most a specified number of nodes remains tractable in relation to that number. The paper presents an algorithm achieving this level of insight in a time proportional to the product of the number of nodes, edges, and the desired number of node breakages. Furthermore, this research extends the previously recognized results for graph invariants such as treewidth and vertex connectivity by providing a corresponding evaluation metric that can be computed in a time also proportional to the product of the number of nodes, edges, and the desired number of node breakages. The approach has been tested on real-world data and compares favorably to existing state-of-the-art methods based on force-directed optimization and local rearrangements. The underlying problem has been found to yield a parameterized problem hard in the sense of being classified as NP-hard in the context of the input parameter, yet easily manageable when considering the size of the input alone. The paper presents a constant-factor approximation algorithm designed to minimize the number of node breakages required to yield an edge-free representation, as well as a more complex exact algorithm both introduced in the paper's proof of excellence section. The research has been applied to a specific case study involving bipartite graphs used for visualizing co-authorship networks. The associated code has been made publicly available as an open-source tool callable from both the command line and as a Python module. The results presented in the paper's figures have been included in the accompanying appendix section. The paper concludes by outlining a number of future research directions presented in the closing section. The paper's main contribution has been recognized as a significant advancement in the field of graph drawing, specifically in the area of bipartite graphs, yet also with broader implications for graph theory in general. Furthermore, we prove that domains with a total residue map are comparable to domains with minimal normalization, as they each possess a property that is equivalent to being finitely unramified within a generic rank one domain. In order to make efficient use of power consumption and heat generation in large-scale cloud servers, a novel approach called HyperDegrade is proposed for optimizing CPU frequency scheduling.  A GPU-accelerated workload is examined and found to be incompatible with existing frequency scheduling methods due to unacceptable performance degradation.  To resolve this issue, a new algorithm called HyperDegrade was developed, which for the first time ever reduces CPU frequency for GPU-accelerated workloads while still achieving significant speedup and energy savings.  In relation to a conventional degradation method, HyperDegrade was found to deliver a 50% performance increase at the same energy efficiency level, or in turn a 25% reduction in energy consumption at the same performance level.  Furthermore, it was observed that a GPU-accelerated deep learning application could be completed 4.6 times faster while using a 50% greater amount of energy.  In addition, HyperDegrade delivers a 2.5 times faster speedup in response to an increase in CPU frequency, and a 4 times faster speedup in response to an increase in the number of GPU cores.  In summary, HyperDegrade provides an efficient CPU frequency scheduling solution for GPU-accelerated workloads, and also provides valuable insights regarding the behavior of performance and energy consumption in cloud servers.  As such, it is hoped that this research will be beneficial to cloud server administrators as well as to researchers in the field of power and temperature awareness.  A working version of HyperDegrade has been made available online for testing purposes.  A note has been added to address the issue of temporary frequency changes, which is relevant to researchers but not directly beneficial to cloud server administrators.  In relation to this, it is hoped that future research will focus on developing more sophisticated models of performance and energy consumption.  A question has also been posed regarding the feasibility of similar degradation methods for other types of accelerated workloads. Kernel methods have proven highly effective in various machine learning applications, yet their scalability to large datasets is severely limited due to the computationally expensive nature of pairwise evaluations. In response, Random Fourier Features were proposed to approximate kernel functions using randomized transformations, thereby enabling the use of kernel methods on larger data sets. While widely adopted, this method has significant drawbacks, notably requiring an unnecessarily large number of features, directly proportional to the size of the dataset, in order to achieve satisfactory results comparable to traditional kernel-based methods. In order to circumvent these limitations and efficiently process large datasets, this paper introduces an alternative method of kernel estimation that leverages insights specific to the underlying data and offers both a newer and more efficient solution, also enabling consistent derivation of features that are data-dependent. We test and evaluate this method against a range of competitors, including RFF, orthogonal random features, and the Nyström method. In order to demonstrate the practical implications of this method for various machine learning applications, we modify popular algorithms to accommodate this method and thoroughly evaluate its performance across multiple benchmarks. In summary, our results show that this method consistently outperforms RFF and yields performance comparable to that of the Nyström method, also offering significant improvements over other methods when evaluating large datasets. In addition to its computational efficiency, this method provides valuable insights into the underlying structure of the data, as demonstrated through both qualitative and quantitative analysis. In contrast to other methods of kernel estimation, this approach is highly versatile and compatible with a wide range of algorithms and scenarios, also offering extensive open-source code available for public use. In summary, this method offers a highly effective and widely applicable solution for the efficient and accurate analysis of large datasets. This research paper examines conformally flat hypersurfaces of n-dimensional space (n is 4 or higher) within a hypersphere of n+2 dimensions. We have obtained two primary results regarding these hypersurfaces. Firstly, under the assumption that one of these hypersurfaces has a non-zero mean curvature, we have proven that it must be isotopic to a sphere defined by a specific equation. Secondly, we have discovered that in dimensions n greater than two, there are exactly two conformally equivalent classes of hypersurfaces with zero mean curvature and constant M\"obius curvature. In particular, this implies that a hypersurface with zero mean curvature and constant scalar curvature in the M\"obius sense is actually a sphere. Additionally, we have established that in dimensions n greater than two, the M\"obius scalar curvature of a compact hypersurface with a non-zero mean curvature is not constant. This, in turn, allows us to provide an alternative proof of an earlier theorem proposed by Burnette and Leitenant. Furthermore, we have discovered that the M\"obius scalar curvature of a compact hypersurface with a non-zero mean curvature is only defined in a relative sense. In other words, two hypersurfaces with different M\"obius scalar curvatures are actually in different conformal classes. This, in turn, enables us to provide an alternative proof of the renamed Fruedenenthal-Burnette-Leitenant theorem. This research was inspired by the aforementioned earlier theorems proposed by Fruedenenthal, Burnette, and Leitenant. In particular, we have discovered that the notion of defined relative M\"obius scalar curvature can be applied to compact hypersurfaces in a space of n+1 dimensions. This, in turn, allows us to provide an alternative proof of the renamed Allen-Wang theorem proposed by Allen and Wang. Additionally, we have discovered that the notion of defined relative M\"obius scalar curvature can be applied to compact hypersurfaces in a space of n+1 dimensions with a non-zero mean curvature with a specific property. This, in turn, enables us to provide an alternative proof of the renamed Chen-Zhen theorem proposed by Chen and Zhen. This research also provides an explicit formula for the M\"obius scalar curvature of a compact hypersurface with a non-zero mean curvature in a space of n+1 dimensions. This, in turn, allows us to provide an alternative proof of the renamed Hu-Wang-Zhou theorem proposed by Hu, Wang, and Zhou

Network vulnerability assessment is crucial for creating strategies to prevent the spread of malicious information and diseases in networks. Researchers often study network immunization, but traditional approaches typically focus on broad measures, such as network criticality and component size. In contrast, this paper delves into a micro-level analysis, where the removal of individual edges or nodes is examined in detail. Based on percolation theory, the authors analyze the effects of removing a single edge in a Cayley tree network structured by a hierarchical system. The results show that the removal of an edge at a specific hierarchy level $k$ leads to the removal of all edges at hierarchy levels $k$ or greater. The distribution of the resulting network fragment is then identified, along with the distribution of the network's component magnitude (i.e. the number of nodes) after the removal of a single edge. The findings are then applied to a variety of network models, including random regular networks, scale-free networks, and networks defined by an edge removal probability. The analysis highlights the importance of examining the effects of removing individual edges or nodes, as the results demonstrate that the removal of a single edge or node at a high hierarchy level can lead to the removal of all nodes at hierarchy levels $k$ or greater. The ability of advanced gravitational wave detectors to perceive high-frequency signals is hindered by the residual noise in the 40-150 Hz range. To address this limitation, a novel concept, the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer, is introduced as an enhancement to the current design by incorporating a non-recycling scheme that involves a optically levitated micro-sphere. This technique succeeds in overcoming the frequency constraint and achieves a signal-to-noise ratio for binary neutron star mergers of approximately 5.5 dB above 120 Hz, also enabling a detection limit for 1.8 solarmass neutron stars at 150 Hz. Furthermore, this idea is highly adaptable to future upgrades or direct detection efforts with a predicted sensitivity for direct detection of gravitational waves from the Sun at 70 Hz. The implementation of a sloshing-Sagnac converter in advanced detectors offers a means of enhancing their low-frequency sensitivity and expanding their capacity to delve into the realm of direct gravitational wave detection. The current proof-of-principle demonstration showcases a signal-to-noise ratio for a solarmass neutron star at 10 Hz of approximately 10 dB, a level that could be reached by future detectors with improved Q factors and increased laser power. The theoretical predictions for this novel design have been verified through actual experimentation, with the achievement of a record signal-to-noise ratio of 13.4 dB for a solarmass neutron star at 10 Hz. The potential applications of the sloshing-Sagnac converter extend beyond gravitational wave detection, also including the detection of nonlinear mechanisms, such as resonant quantum fluctuations and nanomechanical coupling, as well as the reduction of noise caused by laser phase nonlinearity and mechanical instability caused by thermal gradients. The implementation of a signal-recycling scheme with a controlled backaction on the micro-sphere or the environment can further enhance the sensitivity of this converter in these applications. We have also examined the implications of this equation of state for finite nuclei and neutron stars, finding that it is consistent with existing data for finite nuclei but may be challenged by certain low-mass neutron star constraints.
